Dead Island was definitely a massive let down. I played through it to varying degrees as all four characters and I just never found it to be that good. I was mostly sold on Dying Light as soon as I saw a demo. Then I played a demo and ended up buying it as soon as soon as there was a steam sale for it.

My thoughts exactly. Dying Light has some enjoyable elements, but it's hamstrung by awkward combat and crafting. Dying Light does the details right, and it feels like a game that gets out of your way and lets you play. It's interesting to see a zombie game embrace running away as a viable method of dealing with the undead, and as it turns out, running away (and climbing and jumping) can be pretty fun.

It takes some getting used to, but running away is crucial in the early game, which makes a lot of sense. You're really low level, your weapons suck, you have no skills, and you don't really know what you're doing. Besides, if you're really in the midst of the zombie apocalypse, does it really make sense to fight zombies every chance you get?

Definitely one of the better purchases this year.

Life is Strange, well, it really is a mixed bag it seems; It's basically a Telltale-like point and click adventure game but with some really innovative gameplay elements that are deeply tied into the overall story (which is one of the innovative aspects of it), and the setting and characters seem to be really hit or miss. People either seem to absolutely love it or loathe it, with little in between, but if you can get past the setting and characters (or even enjoy those) you're rewarded with a really amazing experience. Plus the game has probably the best voice acting I've ever seen in a video game, bar none, by the same voice actress that did Tiny Tina in Borderlands 2, incidentally, which is amazing considering the difference in tone and character not only between the games but also between the two different characters she voices. Even if everything else about the game was terrible it would still get a special place in gaming history for me because of the way the voice acting performance made a character feel alive in a video game.

Freaking Splatoon, man. I avoided it for a long time, thinking it wouldn't appeal to me. Black friday it was at the store for 25 bucks so I bought it on a whim.

I have played it nearly every day since. It's incredible at how simplistic, yet addictive these 3 minute matches are. The intensity ramps up as the game starts to learn your style of playing and matches you up with other, more "hardcore" gamers, and there is an ever present threat of the momentum shifting up to the final few seconds.

There is a single player mode that was also surprisingly fun. Completing it unlocks weapons and gear that you otherwise might not see much of in the multiplayer game. I'm tickled whenever I see someone wearing gear from the campaign. The challenges in the single player are also super intense, especially the last few bosses.

The multiplayer though, is really fantastic. Super smooth gameplay, I never feel cheated, and they update the game every few weeks/months by adding new stages, weapons, or patching little sneaky glitches people have discovered. If you are sitting on the fence, I definitely recommend trying it out. Hell, just talking about it makes me want to play it. Be back later!

We've used terror to eradicate any hint of privacy. Cointelpro aside, the current generation of young americans has had their entire lives recorded on a scale never before seen. All social webs, data exchanges and interactions cataloged, mined and utilized to reveal more personal information than anyone can generally comprehend without years of marketing analysis experience.

We've used terror to stifle freedom of speech and more frighteningly freedom of thought. The "love it or leave it" mentality of the Bush era has moved full steam into the micro-aggression era. Where we once wouldn't question or speak against our governments decisions without conflicting with nationalism/patriotism; We've now shifted into not questioning inequalities we see everyday because of privilege checking and a hierarchy of marginalized peoples.

I'm not terrified about the one in a million chance of dying in a terrorist attack. I'm terrified by the absolute fact that my government is harvesting yet another atrocity to undermine my freedoms and consolidate power. I'm terrified that fear has won over logic.
